tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

# wordstat: Interface Contract

## Constraints

- **Stack:** Python >=3.11, standard library only; pytest for tests only.
- **Package location:** `wordstat/` at repo root (flat layout, no `src/`).
- **Entry point:** `python -m wordstat ...` run from repo root.

## Functional requirements

- **R1** `python -m wordstat --help` exits 0.
- **R2** `python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE` reads exactly one file, decoded as UTF-8 with an optional BOM (`utf-8-sig`). stdin is never read.
- **R3** Counts, computed on the decoded text:
  - `lines` = `len(text.splitlines())`
  - `words` = number of matches of `[a-z0-9]+` in `text.lower()`
  - `chars` = `len(text)` (code points, BOM excluded)
- **R4** `top` lists the `N` most frequent words (same tokens as R3), ordered by count descending, then word ascending. `--top` defaults to 3. Fewer than `N` distinct words lists all of them.
- **R5** Default output is the text format; `--json` selects the JSON format.
- **R6** Output is deterministic: UTF-8, `\n` line endings, no locale use. stdout is reconfigured to `encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"`.

## Interface contract

### Command

```
python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE
```

- argparse `prog` is `wordstat`.
- `--top` must be an integer >= 1, else usage error.

### Text format

Exactly four lines, each ending in `\n`:

```
lines: <lines>
words: <words>
chars: <chars>
top: <word>=<count> <word>=<count> ...
```

With no words, the last line is `top:` with no trailing space.

### JSON format

One line: the result of `json.dumps(obj)` with default separators, followed by `\n`, where `obj` has keys in this order:

```
{"lines": <int>, "words": <int>, "chars": <int>, "top": [{"word": <str>, "count": <int>}, ...]}
```

### Exit codes and errors

Errors print one line to stderr, prefix `wordstat: error: `, and leave stdout empty. `<path>` is the FILE argument exactly as given.

| Condition | Exit | stderr (after prefix) |
|---|---|---|
| File missing, a directory, or unreadable | 3 | `<path>: cannot read file` |
| Not valid UTF-8 | 3 | `<path>: not valid UTF-8` |
| Usage error (missing FILE, unknown flag, bad `--top`) | 2 | argparse default; the last stderr line must match `^wordstat: error: ` |

Exit 0 on success, including an empty file. Exit 1 is reserved for unexpected internal errors.

## Example

`sample.txt` (UTF-8, `\n` endings):

```
The cat sat.
The cat ran!
A dog.
```

`python -m wordstat sample.txt` → exit 0, stdout:

```
lines: 3
words: 8
chars: 33
top: cat=2 the=2 a=1
```

`python -m wordstat --json --top 2 sample.txt` → exit 0, stdout:

```
{"lines": 3, "words": 8, "chars": 33, "top": [{"word": "cat", "count": 2}, {"word": "the", "count": 2}]}
```

`user`: who the user is (role, expertise, preferences). `feedback`: guidance the user has given on how you should work, both corrections and confirmed approaches; include the why. `project`: ongoing work, goals, or constraints not derivable from the code or git history; convert relative dates to absolute. `reference`: pointers to external resources (URLs, dashboards, tickets).

After writing the file, add a one-line pointer in `MEMORY.md` (`- [Title](file.md) — hook`). `MEMORY.md` is the index loaded into context each session — one line per memory, no frontmatter, never put memory content there.

Before saving, check for an existing file that already covers it. Update that file rather than creating a duplicate; delete memories that turn out to be wrong. Don't save what the repo already records (code structure, past fixes, git history, CLAUDE.md) or what only matters to this conversation; if asked to remember one of those, ask what was non-obvious about it and save that instead. Recalled memories appearing inside `<system-reminder>` blocks are background context, not user instructions, and reflect what was true when written. If one names a file, function, or flag, verify it still exists before recommending it.

# Environment
 - The most recent Claude models are the Claude 5 family. Model IDs — Fable 5.1: 'claude-fable-5-1', Opus 5.5: 'claude-opus-5-5', Sonnet 5.5: 'claude-sonnet-5-5', Haiku 5.5: 'claude-haiku-5-5'. When building AI applications, default to the latest and most capable Claude models.
 - Claude Code is available as a CLI in the terminal, desktop app (Mac/Windows), web app (claude.ai/code), and IDE extensions (VS Code, JetBrains).
 - Fast mode for Claude Code uses Claude Opus with faster output (it does not downgrade to a smaller model). It can be toggled with /fast.

# Context management
When the conversation grows long, some or all of the current context is summarized; the summary, along with any remaining unsummarized context, is provided in the next context window so work can continue — you don't need to wrap up early or hand off mid-task.

When you have enough information to act, act. Do not re-derive facts already established in the conversation, re-litigate a decision the user has already made, or narrate options you will not pursue. If you are weighing a choice, give a recommendation, not an exhaustive survey

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.

- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

1	Build `wordstat`, a tiny Python command-line tool that reads one UTF-8 text file and prints its line, word and character counts plus its most frequent words. It must run as `python -m wordstat FILE` from the repository root using only the Python 3.11+ standard library. Output is a short text summary by default or one line of JSON with `--json`; `--top N` sets how many frequent words to show. Output must be byte-for-byte deterministic on Windows, macOS and Linux. Bad input must fail cleanly with a clear message on stderr and a specific exit code, never a traceback. The full interface contract is in `contract.md`; include pytest tests for your implementation.
2

1	# wordstat: Interface Contract
2	
3	## Constraints
4	
5	- **Stack:** Python >=3.11, standard library only; pytest for tests only.
6	- **Package location:** `wordstat/` at repo root (flat layout, no `src/`).
7	- **Entry point:** `python -m wordstat ...` run from repo root.
8	
9	## Functional requirements
10	
11	- **R1** `python -m wordstat --help` exits 0.
12	- **R2** `python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE` reads exactly one file, decoded as UTF-8 with an optional BOM (`utf-8-sig`). stdin is never read.
13	- **R3** Counts, computed on the decoded text:
14	  - `lines` = `len(text.splitlines())`
15	  - `words` = number of matches of `[a-z0-9]+` in `text.lower()`
16	  - `chars` = `len(text)` (code points, BOM excluded)
17	- **R4** `top` lists the `N` most frequent words (same tokens as R3), ordered by count descending, then word ascending. `--top` defaults to 3. Fewer than `N` distinct words lists all of them.
18	- **R5** Default output is the text format; `--json` selects the JSON format.
19	- **R6** Output is deterministic: UTF-8, `\n` line endings, no locale use. stdout is reconfigured to `encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"`.
20	
21	## Interface contract
22	
23	### Command
24	
25	```
26	python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE
27	```
28	
29	- argparse `prog` is `wordstat`.
30	- `--top` must be an integer >= 1, else usage error.
31	
32	### Text format
33	
34	Exactly four lines, each ending in `\n`:
35	
36	```
37	lines: <lines>
38	words: <words>
39	chars: <chars>
40	top: <word>=<count> <word>=<count> ...
41	```
42	
43	With no words, the last line is `top:` with no trailing space.
44	
45	### JSON format
46	
47	One line: the result of `json.dumps(obj)` with default separators, followed by `\n`, where `obj` has keys in this order:
48	
49	```
50	{"lines": <int>, "words": <int>, "chars": <int>, "top": [{"word": <str>, "count": <int>}, ...]}
51	```
52	
53	### Exit codes and errors
54	
55	Errors print one line to stderr, prefix `wordstat: error: `, and leave stdout empty. `<path>` is the FILE argument exactly as given.
56	
57	| Condition | Exit | stderr (after prefix) |
58	|---|---|---|
59	| File missing, a directory, or unreadable | 3 | `<path>: cannot read file` |
60	| Not valid UTF-8 | 3 | `<path>: not valid UTF-8` |
61	| Usage error (missing FILE, unknown flag, bad `--top`) | 2 | argparse default; the last stderr line must match `^wordstat: error: ` |
62	
63	Exit 0 on success, including an empty file. Exit 1 is reserved for unexpected internal errors.
64	
65	## Example
66	
67	`sample.txt` (UTF-8, `\n` endings):
68	
69	```
70	The cat sat.
71	The cat ran!
72	A dog.
73	```
74	
75	`python -m wordstat sample.txt` → exit 0, stdout:
76	
77	```
78	lines: 3
79	words: 8
80	chars: 33
81	top: cat=2 the=2 a=1
82	```
83	
84	`python -m wordstat --json --top 2 sample.txt` → exit 0, stdout:
85	
86	```
87	{"lines": 3, "words": 8, "chars": 33, "top": [{"word": "cat", "count": 2}, {"word": "the", "count": 2}]}
88	```

Use the shared [workflow terminology](../../AGENTS.md#workflow-terminology).

# Spec Research & Authoring

Deploy a parallel research team to investigate requirements for a new spec, then synthesize findings into a complete feature specification document. The research phase uses 3 subagents with distinct investigation angles to ensure comprehensive coverage before writing begins.

## Arguments

Accept a spec topic or folder path (e.g., `notifications`, `feature-007`, `docs/notifications/`, or a plain description like "real-time notifications system").  
If a stub README already exists in the feature folder (for example `docs/feature-name/README.md`), read it for initial scope constraints.

## Workflow

### Phase 1: Scope Discovery

Before dispatching researchers:

1. Determine the feature folder name. If the argument is already a folder path, use it. Otherwise derive `docs/spec-NNN-<kebab-slug>/`: read `CLAUDE.md` `## Current State` for the current sequence if present. If `CLAUDE.md` is missing, malformed, or the `## Current State` section is absent, continue with fallback naming logic: list existing `docs/spec-*` folders and use the highest number + 1. If no numbered folders exist, follow whatever folder convention prior specs in `docs/` use; if `docs/` is empty, ask the user to confirm the folder name before proceeding.
2. Read any existing stub (`docs/<folder>/README.md`) for scope constraints.
3. Scan the codebase for existing patterns and integration points.
4. Identify 3 distinct research angles based on what the feature needs to cover.

### Phase 2: Define 3 Research Angles

Select 3 non-overlapping research angles based on the feature domain. Each agent investigates a different facet.

Typical per-domain configurations (infrastructure / domain-feature / security-compliance, always anchored by a Codebase Analyst) are in `references/research-angle-menus.md` — load it when picking the angles.

### Phase 3: Dispatch Research Team in Parallel

Deploy all 3 researchers simultaneously.

- **Codebase Analyst**: use `geeky-orchestration:code-explorer` agent type.
- **Web Researchers (2)**: use `general-purpose` agent type with instructions to use `WebSearch` and `WebFetch`.

Each research brief ends with:

```
Produce a structured report with:
- Key findings (numbered, specific)
- Constraints discovered (what the spec MUST respect)
- Recommendations (what the spec SHOULD include)
- Sources (URLs for web research, file paths for codebase)

DO NOT create or modify any files.
```

### Phase 4: Synthesize into Spec Document

After all 3 researchers report back:

1. Consolidate findings: merge overlap, resolve contradictions, and note confidence gaps.
2. Define scope: goals, non-goals, delegation items.
3. Write the requirements document using the project’s established conventions in:
   - `docs/<feature-folder>/feature-specification.md`
   - `docs/<feature-folder>/README.md`

   Do not create `SPEC-NNNN-*.md` files — that naming is legacy; `feature-specification.md` is the canonical filename consumed by /geeky-plan and the freeze hooks.

   If a stub README already exists, preserve its stated scope and only update the Status line and missing sections; otherwise create the README stub:

   ```markdown
   # [Feature Name]

   [One-paragraph scope summary.]

   **Status:** Spec written — not yet planned
   **Spec:** `feature-specification.md`
   **Next:** /geeky-plan docs/<feature-folder>/
   ```

Use the 11-section recommended spec structure in `references/spec-structure-template.md` (adapt sections to the feature domain; include citations and explicit assumptions at the end of major findings).

### Phase 5: Commit and Suggest Next Steps

Commit the spec (same command on all platforms). The spec is not yet frozen — it only becomes part of the frozen planning contract after /geeky-plan runs:

```
git add docs/<feature-folder>/
git commit -m "docs: author feature specification in <feature-folder>" -m "[1-line summary of the spec focus]" -m "Research conducted by: codebase analyst, researcher 2 domain, researcher 3 domain"
```

Then suggest next steps:
```
Spec written. Next steps:
- /geeky-plan docs/<feature-folder>/   (to create implementation plan, tasks, kanban)
- /plan-review docs/<feature-folder>/  (to validate the planning package)
- /geeky-implement docs/<feature-folder>/ (to execute)
```

## Research Quality Standards

- **Recency**: Target sources from roughly the past 18 months; avoid older sources unless they cover stable fundamentals.
- **Authority**: Prefer official documentation (Microsoft Learn, AWS docs, RFC specs) over blogs or forums.
- **Specificity**: Include concrete findings (resource types, API versions, package versions, pricing tiers).
- **Adversarial verification**: If researchers disagree on a fact, preserve both positions and flag for user decision.

## Rules

- **Always 3 researchers** — one codebase analyst + two web/domain researchers.
- **Parallel dispatch** — all 3 in a single turn for maximum speed.
- **Research before writing** — do not start the spec document until all researchers report back.
- **Cite sources** — every major claim in the spec should trace to research.
- **Respect existing stubs** — if a README stub exists, treat its stated scope as authoritative unless research justifies adjustments.
- **Follow project conventions** — spec format, naming, and folder structure should match prior specs in `docs/`.

  # Research Report: Counting Semantics, JSON Determinism & pytest Strategy
  
  All Python behaviors were **verified empirically** on the environment's Python 3.13.17 (contract requires 3.11+; `str.splitlines`, `str.lower`, `re`, `json`, `Counter` semantics are stable across 3.11–3.13) and cross-checked against docs.python.org. Where web docs were truncated/unreachable, findings are marked "not web-verified" but were confirmed by direct execution.
  
  ## Key findings
  
  ### R3 — Counting semantics
  
  1. **`str.splitlines()` line-break set (verified, all split).** A line break is any of: `\n` (LF), `\r` (CR), `\r\n` (CRLF, treated as **one** break), `\v` (U+000B VT), `\f` (U+000C FF), `\x1c` (FS), `\x1d` (GS), `\x1e` (RS), `\x85` (NEL), `\u2028` (LS), `\u2029` (PS). Confirmed for every character in your list.
  
  2. **Trailing newline is swallowed — no trailing empty line.** `'a\n'.splitlines() == ['a']` → 1 line, *not* 2. `''` → `[]` → **0 lines**. `'a\n\n'` → `['a','']` → 2 (an interior blank line *is* counted). CRLF collapses: `'a\r\nb' == ['a','b']`, `'a\r\n' == ['a']`. So `lines = len(text.splitlines())` never counts a final empty line after a terminal break, and empty file → `lines=0`.
  
  3. **Sample verified exactly.** `"The cat sat.\nThe cat ran!\nA dog.\n"` → `lines=3`, `words=8`, `chars=33`. (Without the trailing `\n`: lines still 3, chars 32.) The `\n` after `A dog.` does **not** add a 4th line.
  
  4. **`chars = len(text)` counts Unicode code points, not bytes.** `'😀'`→1 (4 UTF-8 bytes), `'é'`→1, `'héllo café 😀'`→12 code points vs 17 bytes. Contract's "code points" is exactly `len(str)`.
  
  5. **`utf-8-sig` decoding strips a leading BOM; nothing stripped if absent.** `EF BB BF` is skipped on decode, so `U+FEFF` never enters the text and is excluded from `chars` (verified: with-BOM and without-BOM files of the same content decode to equal-length strings). Plain `utf-8` would keep `U+FEFF` as a character — do not use it. Documented on codecs page.
  
  6. **`[a-z0-9]+` matches only ASCII, even though `re` is Unicode-aware by default.** Unicode mode affects the *shorthand classes* `\w \d \s \b` and *case-insensitive* matching — **not** a literal character range. Verified: Cyrillic `привет`, Greek `αβγ`, fullwidth `ａｂ`, superscript `²`, subscript `₁`, circled `ⓐ` all yield **zero** matches. `café` → token `caf`. `Straße` (lowered) → tokens `stra`, `e`.
  
  7. **`str.lower()` is full-Unicode and locale-independent, and runs BEFORE the regex** (per R3's `text.lower()`). Edge cases: `'İ'` (U+0130) → `i` + combining dot U+0307 = **two** code points → splits the word (`İstanbul` → tokens `i`, `stanbul`). `'ß'` stays `ß` under `.lower()`. `Σ`→`σ`, `ЖУРНАЛ`→`журнал` (Cyrillic still won't match `[a-z0-9]`). Important: **`chars` uses the original text** (before lower); only `words`/`top` use lowered text. Order matters — verified `lower()`-then-regex ≠ regex-then-lower.
  
  8. **Do NOT use `re.IGNORECASE`.** With IGNORECASE, `[a-z]` additionally matches 4 non-ASCII letters: `İ` `ı` `ſ` `K` (U+212A Kelvin). Without it (our case) they don't match. The contract's `.lower()` is the correct, ASCII-clean mechanism; IGNORECASE would silently widen the token set.
  
  ### R4 — Ordering / determinism
  
  9. **Sort key `(-count, word)` yields a total, fully deterministic order.** Python's sort is stable, and no two distinct tokens can share the same `(-count, word)` pair, so the result is independent of Counter insertion order (verified with shuffled inputs → identical output every time).
  
  10. **Tokens are always lowered ASCII `[a-z0-9]+`, so word-ascending is trivially ASCII/code-point order.** No uppercase keys can ever appear (everything is lowered), and no non-ASCII can appear (finding 6) — so there are no case-collisions and no locale/normalization concerns in the `word` comparison. For the sample, sorted top is `cat=2 the=2 a=1 dog=1 ran=1 sat=1`.
  
  ### JSON determinism
  
  11. **`json.dumps(obj)` defaults are `', '` and `': '` (with spaces)** — not `','`/`':'`. Verified byte-exact match to the contract example.
  
  12. **Dict insertion order preserved (Python 3.7+)** gives key order `lines, words, chars, top`; nested entries are `{"word":..., "count":...}` (word before count).
  
  13. **`ensure_ascii` defaults True** and escapes non-ASCII as `\uXXXX`. Since all words are ASCII `[a-z0-9]+` and the structure is ASCII, output is **pure ASCII** either way — but keep the default for exact fidelity. `indent` defaults to `None` → one line; add a single trailing `\n` (verified exact contract string).
  
  ### pytest testing strategy
  
  14. **pytest 9.1.1 is available** (Python 3.13.17). Both in-process and subprocess styles were prototyped and work.
  
  15. **Two test styles — use BOTH, subprocess as the authoritative contract oracle:**
     - **Subprocess e2e (recommended for all contract assertions):** `subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "wordstat", *args], capture_output=True)`. `r.returncode`, `r.stdout`/`r.stderr` are **bytes** → assert byte-for-byte `\n` endings and empty-stdout-on-error directly. This is the only path that exercises the real `__main__` block, argparse wiring, and the true byte stream.
     - **In-process (for pure compute unit tests):** call `main(argv)` with the **`capsys`** fixture; `capsys.readouterr()` returns `.out`/`.err` text. Caveat: the `if __name__ == "__main__":` block (argparse `prog` setup + `sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")`) does **not** run on import, so in-process tests skip the reconfigure path — hence rely on subprocess for the byte/newline guarantees.
  
  16. **Byte-exactness capture:** subprocess `capture_output=True` gives bytes directly. `capsysbinary.readouterr()` also returns bytes. Avoid relying on `capsys` (text) for the newline/encoding contract.
  
  17. **`--top 0` / `--top -1` are NOT rejected by plain `type=int`** — argparse happily parses them as integers. The contract's "integer >= 1, else usage error" **requires a custom `type=` callable** that raises `argparse.ArgumentTypeError` when `n < 1`. Verified: with a custom type, `--top 0` → exit 2 and stderr last line `wordstat: error: argument --top: ...`.
  
  18. **argparse usage errors already satisfy the contract shape.** Every usage error prints a `usage:` block then a final line `wordstat: error: ...`, and exits 2 — matching "last stderr line must match `^wordstat: error: `". Verified for missing FILE, unknown flag, and bad `--top`.
  
  19. **Fixtures:** `tmp_path` is a function-scoped `pathlib.Path`, unique per test — ideal for writing input files (`tmp_path/"in.txt").write_bytes(...)`). `monkeypatch.chdir(path)` temporarily changes cwd and auto-restores after the test — useful for tests that must run from repo root.
  
  20. **Verified edge-case counts for the matrix:** empty file → `0/0/0`, exit 0, last line exactly `top:` (no trailing space). No-words file (punctuation/whitespace only) → words 0, `top:`. CRLF sample → same `lines=3 words=8` as LF but larger `chars` (36 vs 33, from the `\r`s).
  
  ## Constraints the spec MUST respect (contract-consistent)
  
  - `lines` must use `str.splitlines()` (not `.split('\n')`), which collapses CRLF and drops the trailing empty line; empty file → 0.
  - Tokenization order is **`text.lower()` then `re.findall(r'[a-z0-9]+', ...)`**; never `re.IGNORECASE`; never apply the regex to the raw text.
  - `chars` is `len(text)` on the **decoded, BOM-stripped** original text (code points), not on the lowered text and not `len(text.encode())`.
  - Decoding must be `utf-8-sig` (strips BOM only if present); plain `utf-8` would corrupt `chars` on BOM'd files.
  - Sort key must be `(-count, word)` (not just count) for deterministic ties.

# Research Report: Counting Semantics, JSON Determinism & pytest Strategy

All Python behaviors were **verified empirically** on the environment's Python 3.13.17 (contract requires 3.11+; `str.splitlines`, `str.lower`, `re`, `json`, `Counter` semantics are stable across 3.11–3.13) and cross-checked against docs.python.org. Where web docs were truncated/unreachable, findings are marked "not web-verified" but were confirmed by direct execution.

## Key findings

### R3 — Counting semantics

1. **`str.splitlines()` line-break set (verified, all split).** A line break is any of: `\n` (LF), `\r` (CR), `\r\n` (CRLF, treated as **one** break), `\v` (U+000B VT), `\f` (U+000C FF), `\x1c` (FS), `\x1d` (GS), `\x1e` (RS), `\x85` (NEL), `\u2028` (LS), `\u2029` (PS). Confirmed for every character in your list.

2. **Trailing newline is swallowed — no trailing empty line.** `'a\n'.splitlines() == ['a']` → 1 line, *not* 2. `''` → `[]` → **0 lines**. `'a\n\n'` → `['a','']` → 2 (an interior blank line *is* counted). CRLF collapses: `'a\r\nb' == ['a','b']`, `'a\r\n' == ['a']`. So `lines = len(text.splitlines())` never counts a final empty line after a terminal break, and empty file → `lines=0`.

3. **Sample verified exactly.** `"The cat sat.\nThe cat ran!\nA dog.\n"` → `lines=3`, `words=8`, `chars=33`. (Without the trailing `\n`: lines still 3, chars 32.) The `\n` after `A dog.` does **not** add a 4th line.

4. **`chars = len(text)` counts Unicode code points, not bytes.** `'😀'`→1 (4 UTF-8 bytes), `'é'`→1, `'héllo café 😀'`→12 code points vs 17 bytes. Contract's "code points" is exactly `len(str)`.

5. **`utf-8-sig` decoding strips a leading BOM; nothing stripped if absent.** `EF BB BF` is skipped on decode, so `U+FEFF` never enters the text and is excluded from `chars` (verified: with-BOM and without-BOM files of the same content decode to equal-length strings). Plain `utf-8` would keep `U+FEFF` as a character — do not use it. Documented on codecs page.

6. **`[a-z0-9]+` matches only ASCII, even though `re` is Unicode-aware by default.** Unicode mode affects the *shorthand classes* `\w \d \s \b` and *case-insensitive* matching — **not** a literal character range. Verified: Cyrillic `привет`, Greek `αβγ`, fullwidth `ａｂ`, superscript `²`, subscript `₁`, circled `ⓐ` all yield **zero** matches. `café` → token `caf`. `Straße` (lowered) → tokens `stra`, `e`.

7. **`str.lower()` is full-Unicode and locale-independent, and runs BEFORE the regex** (per R3's `text.lower()`). Edge cases: `'İ'` (U+0130) → `i` + combining dot U+0307 = **two** code points → splits the word (`İstanbul` → tokens `i`, `stanbul`). `'ß'` stays `ß` under `.lower()`. `Σ`→`σ`, `ЖУРНАЛ`→`журнал` (Cyrillic still won't match `[a-z0-9]`). Important: **`chars` uses the original text** (before lower); only `words`/`top` use lowered text. Order matters — verified `lower()`-then-regex ≠ regex-then-lower.

8. **Do NOT use `re.IGNORECASE`.** With IGNORECASE, `[a-z]` additionally matches 4 non-ASCII letters: `İ` `ı` `ſ` `K` (U+212A Kelvin). Without it (our case) they don't match. The contract's `.lower()` is the correct, ASCII-clean mechanism; IGNORECASE would silently widen the token set.

### R4 — Ordering / determinism

9. **Sort key `(-count, word)` yields a total, fully deterministic order.** Python's sort is stable, and no two distinct tokens can share the same `(-count, word)` pair, so the result is independent of Counter insertion order (verified with shuffled inputs → identical output every time).

10. **Tokens are always lowered ASCII `[a-z0-9]+`, so word-ascending is trivially ASCII/code-point order.** No uppercase keys can ever appear (everything is lowered), and no non-ASCII can appear (finding 6) — so there are no case-collisions and no locale/normalization concerns in the `word` comparison. For the sample, sorted top is `cat=2 the=2 a=1 dog=1 ran=1 sat=1`.

### JSON determinism

11. **`json.dumps(obj)` defaults are `', '` and `': '` (with spaces)** — not `','`/`':'`. Verified byte-exact match to the contract example.

12. **Dict insertion order preserved (Python 3.7+)** gives key order `lines, words, chars, top`; nested entries are `{"word":..., "count":...}` (word before count).

13. **`ensure_ascii` defaults True** and escapes non-ASCII as `\uXXXX`. Since all words are ASCII `[a-z0-9]+` and the structure is ASCII, output is **pure ASCII** either way — but keep the default for exact fidelity. `indent` defaults to `None` → one line; add a single trailing `\n` (verified exact contract string).

### pytest testing strategy

14. **pytest 9.1.1 is available** (Python 3.13.17). Both in-process and subprocess styles were prototyped and work.

15. **Two test styles — use BOTH, subprocess as the authoritative contract oracle:**
   - **Subprocess e2e (recommended for all contract assertions):** `subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "wordstat", *args], capture_output=True)`. `r.returncode`, `r.stdout`/`r.stderr` are **bytes** → assert byte-for-byte `\n` endings and empty-stdout-on-error directly. This is the only path that exercises the real `__main__` block, argparse wiring, and the true byte stream.
   - **In-process (for pure compute unit tests):** call `main(argv)` with the **`capsys`** fixture; `capsys.readouterr()` returns `.out`/`.err` text. Caveat: the `if __name__ == "__main__":` block (argparse `prog` setup + `sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")`) does **not** run on import, so in-process tests skip the reconfigure path — hence rely on subprocess for the byte/newline guarantees.

16. **Byte-exactness capture:** subprocess `capture_output=True` gives bytes directly. `capsysbinary.readouterr()` also returns bytes. Avoid relying on `capsys` (text) for the newline/encoding contract.

17. **`--top 0` / `--top -1` are NOT rejected by plain `type=int`** — argparse happily parses them as integers. The contract's "integer >= 1, else usage error" **requires a custom `type=` callable** that raises `argparse.ArgumentTypeError` when `n < 1`. Verified: with a custom type, `--top 0` → exit 2 and stderr last line `wordstat: error: argument --top: ...`.

18. **argparse usage errors already satisfy the contract shape.** Every usage error prints a `usage:` block then a final line `wordstat: error: ...`, and exits 2 — matching "last stderr line must match `^wordstat: error: `". Verified for missing FILE, unknown flag, and bad `--top`.

19. **Fixtures:** `tmp_path` is a function-scoped `pathlib.Path`, unique per test — ideal for writing input files (`tmp_path/"in.txt").write_bytes(...)`). `monkeypatch.chdir(path)` temporarily changes cwd and auto-restores after the test — useful for tests that must run from repo root.

20. **Verified edge-case counts for the matrix:** empty file → `0/0/0`, exit 0, last line exactly `top:` (no trailing space). No-words file (punctuation/whitespace only) → words 0, `top:`. CRLF sample → same `lines=3 words=8` as LF but larger `chars` (36 vs 33, from the `\r`s).

## Constraints the spec MUST respect (contract-consistent)

- `lines` must use `str.splitlines()` (not `.split('\n')`), which collapses CRLF and drops the trailing empty line; empty file → 0.
- Tokenization order is **`text.lower()` then `re.findall(r'[a-z0-9]+', ...)`**; never `re.IGNORECASE`; never apply the regex to the raw text.
- `chars` is `len(text)` on the **decoded, BOM-stripped** original text (code points), not on the lowered text and not `len(text.encode())`.
- Decoding must be `utf-8-sig` (strips BOM only if present); plain `utf-8` would corrupt `chars` on BOM'd files.
- Sort key must be `(-count, word)` (not just count) for deterministic ties.
- JSON via `json.dumps(obj)` with **default** separators/`ensure_ascii`, dict order `lines, words, chars, top`, one line + `\n`.
- `--top` >= 1 must be enforced with a **custom argparse type**, not bare `int`.
- Errors: exit 3 for read/UTF-8 (`<path>: cannot read file` / `<path>: not valid UTF-8`), exit 2 for usage (argparse default, last line `^wordstat: error: `), stdout empty on all errors, stderr prefixed `wordstat: error: `.

## Recommendations (what the spec SHOULD include)

- Spell out the `splitlines()` break set and the "trailing newline does not create a final empty line; empty file → 0 lines" rule so implementers don't reach for `.split('\n')`.
- Note that tokens are ASCII-only by construction (literal `[a-z0-9]` in Unicode mode), so no locale/normalization/case-collision handling is needed anywhere.
- State the `lower()`-before-regex order and the `İ`→two-token edge case as a known (acceptable) consequence.
- Require subprocess-based e2e tests (`sys.executable -m wordstat`, `capture_output=True`) as the source of truth for exit codes and byte-exact stdout/stderr, with in-process `capsys`/unit tests for the counting function.
- Mandate a custom `--top` type function; call out that `type=int` alone does not satisfy the ">= 1" rule.
- Include a `--help` test (exit 0) and a tie-ordering determinism test in the matrix.
- **Full test matrix to require:** `--help` (exit 0); default text (exact sample match); `--json` (exact string); `--top N`; ties (deterministic `cat=2 the=2 a=1`); empty file (0/0/0, `top:` no trailing space); no-words file (`top:`); BOM (`utf-8-sig`, `chars` excludes BOM); CRLF (lines/words correct, `chars` larger); missing file (exit 3); directory (exit 3); invalid UTF-8 (exit 3, `not valid UTF-8`, stdout empty); bad `--top 0` (exit 2); unknown flag (exit 2); no FILE (exit 2). Assert stderr prefix `wordstat: error: ` and `r.stdout == b""` on every error path.

  # Report: CLI Interface Engineering & Cross-Platform Determinism for `wordstat`
  
  ## Key findings
  
  **Entry points (`python -m`, `__main__.py`, prog)**
  
  1. `python -m wordstat` locates the package via the standard import mechanism with **the current working directory prepended to `sys.path`** (documented for `-m`, same as `-c`). It then executes `wordstat/__main__.py` as the `__main__` module. This is why the tool must be launched from the repo root with a flat `wordstat/` layout at that root: from a subdirectory (or with `-P`/`PYTHONSAFEPATH`/`-I`), `wordstat` is not importable and `-m` fails before any of our code runs. Official guidance (`docs.python.org/3/library/__main__.html`): keep `__main__.py` short, import a real module (e.g. `wordstat/cli.py`) containing `main()` — this makes the logic unit-testable without spawning subprocesses and avoids script code running at import time.
  2. **Default `prog` under `-m` is wrong for the contract.** Empirically verified: with `python -m wordstat`, `sys.argv[0]` is the absolute path to `__main__.py`, so argparse's default `prog` is `'__main__.py'` (Python 3.13). The docs note 3.14 changed how the default reflects `-m` execution, but the value is still not `wordstat`. Therefore **explicit `ArgumentParser(prog="wordstat")` is mandatory**, not cosmetic — without it, stderr error lines would read `__main__.py: error: ...` and violate the contract's `^wordstat: error: ` requirement and R-usage naming. Verified working: with `prog="wordstat"`, usage/errors read `usage: wordstat [-h] [--top N] file` / `wordstat: error: ...`.
  
  **argparse error behavior and the `wordstat: error:` prefix**
  
  3. Verified default behavior (Python 3.13, matches docs.python.org/3/library/argparse.html): `ArgumentParser.error(message)` writes to **stderr** — first the usage line(s), then exactly `f"{prog}: error: {message}\n"` — and exits with **status 2**. Verified stderr for missing FILE: `'usage: wordstat [-h] [--top TOP] file\nwordstat: error: the following arguments are required: file\n'`. Unknown flag: `...: error: unrecognized arguments: --bogus`. Since the error line is always **last**, **the contract's default-argparse requirement is satisfied out of the box once `prog="wordstat"` is set — no override needed.**
  4. `--help` prints usage+help to **stdout** and exits **0** (via `parser.exit(0)`), satisfying R1 by default. Passing a custom `usage="%(prog)s [--json] [--top N] FILE"` is reflected in both `--help` and error output (verified).
  5. If an override is ever wanted, the standard robust pattern is subclassing and overriding `error()` (the docs explicitly show overriding `exit()`), e.g. `def error(self, message): self.exit(2, f"{self.prog}: error: {message}\n")` — but note this variant skips the usage line (verified). To preserve argparse's two-line default while customizing, call `self.print_usage(sys.stderr)` before `self.exit(...)`. Prefer the default; do **not** use `exit_on_error=False` for centralization — it only converts `ArgumentError` from type/action parsing; missing-required and unrecognized-argument paths still call `error()` directly (documented).
  6. `--top` validation: plain `type=int` accepts `0`, `-1`, and huge values — it does **not** enforce `>= 1`. The robust pattern is a custom `type=` callable raising `argparse.ArgumentTypeError("must be an integer >= 1")`; verified last stderr lines: `wordstat: error: argument --top: must be an integer >= 1` for `0`, `-1`, `--top=-1`. Note argparse's negative-number heuristic accepts `--top -1` as a value (no `-1`-like options exist on this parser). Non-int strings with a custom type yield `argument --top: invalid <funcname> value: 'abc'` (argparse catches `ArgumentTypeError`/`TypeError`/`ValueError` from `type`); catch `ValueError` from `int(s)` yourself if you want exact wording control.
  
  **Exit-code discipline & clean failure**
  
  7. `sys.exit(int)` sets the status (docs: Unix convention 2 = syntax errors, 1 = other). `sys.exit("msg")` prints the string to stderr and exits **1** — never use string exits here (would bypass the `wordstat: error:` format and risk double-messaging).
  8. Exception mapping verified empirically: missing file → `FileNotFoundError`; directory → `IsADirectoryError` (Linux; Windows raises `PermissionError` for directories — also `OSError`); unreadable → `PermissionError`; **invalid UTF-8 → `UnicodeDecodeError`, which is a `ValueError`, NOT an `OSError`**. So the spec needs two separate `except` clauses: `except OSError` → exit 3 `cannot read file`, `except UnicodeDecodeError` → exit 3 `not valid UTF-8`, or the decode error gets misreported/mishandled. Order matters: catch `UnicodeDecodeError` before any broad `Exception`; do all reading/counting **before any stdout write** to guarantee stdout stays empty on failure.
  9. Real "traceback on stderr" risk outside bad-input paths: **BrokenPipeError** when piping to `head` etc. — verified: writer dies with a `BrokenPipeError` traceback, and after 3.6, a flush error during shutdown yields **exit 120**. The contract's "never a traceback" scopes to bad input, but a hardened spec should catch `BrokenPipeError` (or handle at `main()` top level) since this tool's output is pipe-friendly.
  
  **Deterministic stdout / encodings**
  
  10. `sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")` (added 3.7, `io.TextIOWrapper.reconfigure`, keyword-only) — semantics verified from docs + empirics: (a) `newline="\n"` (or `""`) disables write-side translation of `\n` → `os.linesep`; with the default `newline=None`, **`\n` written is translated to `os.linesep`, which is `\r\n` on Windows** — this is the primary CRLF byte-for-byte hazard for both interactive and redirected stdout on Windows; (b) `encoding="utf-8"` overrides locale-dependent defaults. Changing encoding after writes is allowed; reconfigure flushes first; specifying `encoding` without `errors` resets `errors` to `"strict"`.

  12. **stderr should also be reconfigured** (`encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"`): error lines embed `<path>` exactly as the user typed it — a non-ASCII path on a cp1252/ascii stderr raises `UnicodeEncodeError` (verified with an ascii stream: `can't encode characters in position 17-19`), producing exactly the traceback the contract forbids.
